newsitem.title: GREECE: GREEK INDUSTRIALISTS SLAM NEW BUDGET'S TAX TARGETS.
newsitem.headline: GREEK INDUSTRIALISTS SLAM NEW BUDGET'S TAX TARGETS.

text.p: Greek industrialists slammed on Wednesday the socialist government's planned budget as shortsighted for seeking quick tax gains while leaving the spendthrift public sector largely intact.

Although the budget will be officially presented at the end of the month, Greek Prime Minister Costas Simitis has outlined its main targets, primarily fiscal recovery through increased tax revenues and some cuts in state spending.

"Once again fiscal adjustment is going to be attempted by measures aiming at the revenue side and tax collecting, leaving largely intact the ultimate causes of the crisis," said Jason Stratos, president of the Federation of Greek Industries.

Greece must drastically limit its large public sector and the huge expenditure requirements it generates in order to catch up with other European Union partners, Stratos told a British- Greek chamber of commerce conference.
The only EU member that has not fulfilled a single Maastricht requirement for economic and moneraty union, Greece has made EU convergence its prime national policy target.
Its main hurdles are a huge foreign and domestic debt, at about 110 percent of GDP and inflation running at about three times the EU average.
Stratos said that Greek industrialists had supported efforts to broaden the tax base and combat tax dodging to rein in the booming black economy.
"But the measures announced are in effect new taxes on the existing tax base, which is already heavily burdened," he said.
The government has said it will abolish most tax breaks, while new taxes will be imposed on government bonds, interbank transactions and other banking products.

"These new taxes, some of which are on capital and not income, may have adverse side-effects of crucial indicators such as savings, interest rates and investment, making real and nominal convergence even more difficult," he said.

He said that Greece's ability to attract foreign investment will be damaged if the message to international markets is that tax rates are on the rise while they are falling in most other EU countries.
"This undoubtedly gives the wrong message to the markets that need a stable tax system in order to plan their activities," Stratos said.

But even if the tax-collecting measures work, they will not provide a lasting solution to fiscal problems. This could come only from drastic cuts in public spending and a re-distribution of funds from consumption to investment.
"Public spending, along with EU funds, should be used for the drastic improvement of infrastructure," Stratos said. "This is the most important prerequisite for growth."
